tweets.text:
AI Is Beginning to Search Beyond Existing Knowledge

Sony AI has introduced Hakken, a system designed to predict scientific relationships that have not yet been documented. The important development is not simply that an AI can search, summarize, or combine published research. Hakken attempts to identify gaps in scientific knowledge and generate specific hypotheses about what may occupy those gaps.

The system converts scientific literature into a temporal knowledge graph. Scientific concepts become nodes, documented relationships become connections, and changes in the graph are tracked over time. A transformer-based model then combines the structure of that graph with the semantic knowledge of a large language model. It looks for patterns indicating that a currently undocumented relationship may nevertheless exist.

In biomedical research, Hakken scored approximately 1.54 million hypotheses related to aging that exceeded its confidence thresholds. Automated filtering reduced this collection to roughly 2,800 candidates. Biomedical experts then selected three hypotheses for laboratory testing by an independent contract research organization.

Two of those three hypotheses received experimental support. The tests identified previously undocumented relationships between TP53 and BAMBI and between RAF1 and TNF. The third proposed relationship, between SOAT1 and STAT3, was not supported under the tested conditions.

These results do not mean that two-thirds of Hakken’s 1.54 million predictions are correct. The three tested hypotheses were selected from a heavily filtered collection and were chosen partly through expert judgment. The result instead demonstrates that an AI system can help locate valuable experimental targets inside an enormous space of possibilities.

That is still a significant development.

Intelligence Is More Than Stored Knowledge

A database can store millions of scientific facts without understanding which facts matter to a particular question. A search engine can retrieve papers containing specified words without recognizing a scientifically important relationship that no paper has explicitly described.

Intelligence requires more than memory. It requires an ability to navigate knowledge: selecting relevant information, recognizing relationships, detecting contradictions, locating gaps, and determining which possible connections deserve investigation.

Hakken provides an early implementation of this distinction. Its value does not come merely from possessing more information than an individual scientist. Its value comes from organizing that information relationally and using the resulting structure to search for missing knowledge.

This suggests that the unit of knowledge is not always the isolated fact. Relationships between facts can be equally important. A sufficiently rich network of known relationships may contain patterns pointing toward relationships that remain unknown.

Scientific Discovery as Abductive Inference

Deduction determines what must follow from accepted premises. Induction identifies regularities from observed examples. Abduction proposes the most plausible explanation or missing relationship capable of making the available evidence fit together.

Much of scientific discovery is abductive. A scientist notices several observations, proposes an unseen mechanism that could connect them, and then designs an experiment to determine whether that mechanism exists.

Hakken automates part of this process. It does not prove its proposed relationships from existing literature. Instead, it detects patterns suggesting that a relationship is plausible enough to test. The output is therefore not established knowledge. It is a prioritized hypothesis.

That distinction is essential. A confident prediction does not become a scientific fact merely because an advanced model produced it. The hypothesis must confront physical reality.

Reality Remains the Final Evaluator

Ideas, theories, mathematical models, knowledge graphs, and AI predictions are maps of reality. Their value depends upon how accurately their implications correspond with what actually happens.

Hakken’s proposed TP53–BAMBI and RAF1–TNF relationships became scientifically meaningful because experiments detected the predicted effects. The unsupported SOAT1–STAT3 prediction was also valuable because reality supplied corrective information.

The complete reasoning cycle is therefore:

Organize existing knowledge, locate a gap, generate a hypothesis, explain the supporting relationships, test the prediction against reality, and update the knowledge system.

The experiment is not an optional addition to machine reasoning. It is the mechanism that separates a plausible conceptual relationship from reliable empirical knowledge.

Functionality Can Produce Greater System-Level Intelligence

Hakken also illustrates how making an AI system more functional can make the entire system more intelligent.

The underlying language model did not accomplish the task alone. It was combined with a temporal knowledge graph, graph-learning models, relation prediction, confidence calibration, an explanation system, automated filtering, expert evaluation, laboratory testing, and empirical feedback.

The resulting intelligence belongs to the architecture as a whole. It emerges from the coordination of memory, representation, prediction, explanation, judgment, action, and correction.

This is important for artificial-intelligence development. Progress may not depend exclusively on building a single, increasingly powerful language model. Significant advances may come from constructing cognitive systems around language models: structured memory, specialized reasoning modules, planning processes, external tools, evaluators, experiments, and feedback loops.

A model can become more capable through scale. A system can become more intelligent through organization.

From Static Libraries to Active Knowledge Systems

A traditional library preserves information and makes it available for retrieval. An active knowledge system would do something more. It would organize ideas according to their relationships, identify which principles apply to a new question, reveal tensions among them, and search for conclusions that have not yet been explicitly stated.

Such a system would not merely answer questions from stored knowledge. It would examine the structure of knowledge before reasoning, determine which conceptual tools are relevant, and identify what remains missing.

Hakken demonstrates a scientific version of that possibility. Its knowledge graph is not simply an archive of biomedical facts. It becomes a navigable representation through which missing connections can be predicted.

This points toward a broader architecture for machine intelligence: structured knowledge available before reasoning, multiple inference methods selected according to the problem, explanations that expose the path behind a conclusion, and an evaluation stage that compares predictions with reality.

The Emerging Human - Machine Discovery System

Hakken is not an autonomous scientist. Human researchers defined the domain, constructed the data pipeline, chose the most interesting hypotheses, designed the experiments, and interpreted the results. The system also predicts relatively simple relationships between scientific concepts rather than producing complete causal theories.

The accomplishment therefore belongs to a human–machine discovery system. Machine inference searches a space too large for individual researchers to navigate. Human judgment determines which possibilities are meaningful. Experiments allow reality to decide which predictions survive.

This division of labor could substantially accelerate science. The limiting factor may gradually shift from finding possible hypotheses to selecting which hypotheses deserve scarce laboratory time, funding, and human attention.

Future systems could extend the loop further by proposing experimental designs, operating automated laboratories, interpreting results, revising their models, and generating the next round of hypotheses. At that point, the system would not merely assist isolated discoveries. It would participate continuously in the process through which scientific knowledge evolves.

Hakken does not establish that fully autonomous scientific intelligence has arrived. The paper is a new preprint, the experimental sample is extremely small, and independent replication remains necessary. It nevertheless demonstrates an important transition.

Artificial intelligence is beginning to move from retrieving what is already known toward navigating the structure of knowledge, identifying what may be missing, and directing experiments toward potentially discoverable truths.

That is a movement from artificial memory toward machine inference and eventually, perhaps, toward engineered scientific intelligence.

Economy Minister Dr @CArchibald_SF has welcomed the publication of a @ucddublin research report, which was co-funded by @Economy_NI, entitled “Use of AI in the Workplace”.

The report provides the first large-scale evidence on the adoption and impact of Generative AI (GenAI) among workers across the island of Ireland. The report examines who is using GenAI, how it is being used, its effects on productivity and job quality, and whether appropriate governance and training arrangements are in place.

It is the first of a number of reports that will flow from the Working in Ireland Survey which, for the first time, provides important employee perspectives on an all-island basis.
